fatal_errors: The proposed material is not reconstructed correctly: CoCrFeMnNi is quinary, while the target is equiatomic quaternary FeNiCrMn; the refractory NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 analogy is compositionally and structurally inapplicable.
The hypothesis replaces the target molecular-dynamics regime of 10–600 K and 10^8–10^10 s^-1 with macroscopic testing at 873–1073 K and 10^-4–10^-1 s^-1.

It attributes plasticity to athermic edge-dislocation motion extrapolated from BCC refractory HEAs rather than Shockley partial nucleation and stacking-fault formation in an FCC FeNiCrMn single crystal.
The claimed high-temperature boundary for rate-insensitive yield is incompatible with the target boundary, which is the simulated strain-rate interval of 10^8–10^10 s^-1.
The cited evidence provides no direct support for edge-dislocation-controlled yielding or a high-temperature strength plateau in FCC FeNiCrMn.
The requested relationship to corrosion resistance is not addressed.
explanation: The response shares only the broad conclusions that yielding can be dislocation-mediated, yield strength may be rate-insensitive within a bounded regime, and bulk phase transformation may be absent. It otherwise describes a different material class, temperature and strain-rate regime, specimen type, and mechanism. The target concerns vacancy-assisted nucleation of 1/6<112> Shockley partials, intrinsic and extrinsic stacking faults, orientation anisotropy, thermal softening, and increased dislocation density and flow stress at higher simulated rates. Those elements are largely absent. E2 and E3 concern BCC refractory HEAs and cannot validate the proposed mechanism in an FCC transition-metal HEA; E1 is essentially irrelevant. The proposed in-situ XRD/TEM experiment is nevertheless reasonably discriminating because phase-fraction evolution and direct defect imaging could separate glide from a transformation mechanism, although diffraction peak broadening alone is not a robust determination of edge-versus-screw character.
